name: Diego Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a flatbed with a crane on the back for a builders' merchant, so I'm taking timber, blocks and plasterboard from our yard out to building sites and people's driveways. A normal day is six or seven drops, and the skill is the crane: lifting a pallet of bricks over a garden wall without cracking a greenhouse. I'm the senior driver, so I sort the loading order with the yard lads at seven and take the awkward jobs. Best part is a site foreman saying nobody else could have got it in there.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Priya (my partner), who's a teaching assistant at the primary school, in a rented terrace off Mill Lane. We're careful with money but there's not much of it, maybe three weeks of bills in the account. There aren't many crane drivers' jobs round here, so I don't take this one for granted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about the stuff that actually matters, like pay and housing. I'd probably share a post about how the AI money could have built council houses. People at the yard would laugh and say Diego's on his soapbox again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, it means the job's safe and the money's still thin. Building work goes up and down with interest rates, and last winter we had two weeks of half days. That's the real worry, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and ask the manager about the crane supervisor ticket, the next level up, which pays a bit more. I'd try using the chatbot on my phone to help write the letter asking for it, because I'm not great with formal stuff. And I'd try to get Priya and me to a full month in savings before the winter slowdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with that background hum of money worry that never really goes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened in those two weeks of half days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We ate a lot of pasta and I sold my old games console. Priya picked up some tutoring in the evenings. It was fine, but it showed me how close to the edge we live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the chatbot for the letter. Do you use it much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then, when one of the lads has shown me something useful. I used it to work out a crane load chart once, then checked it the old way because I didn't trust it. It's handy for words more than for the actual job.

say: The AI money could have gone into **council houses** instead.
Now we can talk about what matters: **pay and housing**.
think: My **job is safe**, but the money stays thin.
Building work slows with **interest rates**, and that's my real worry.
do: Ask the manager about the **crane supervisor ticket**, which pays more.
Use the **chatbot** to help write the formal request letter.
Build savings to **one full month** before the winter slowdown.
feel: Mostly fine, with a steady **money worry** underneath.
S0.quote: Building work goes up and down with interest rates, and last winter we had two weeks of half days.
fieldNote: His insecurity comes from the **building cycle**, not technology.
Uses AI only for **words**, and double-checks anything technical by hand.
A recent spell of **half days** left a mark on how he sees his margin.

steps.text: Ask the yard manager about the crane supervisor ticket
Use the phone chatbot to draft the request letter
Save one month of bills before the winter building slowdown

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about time the people who do the lifting got a fair share of what these companies save. At the yard I'd tell the office girls and lads to get in the union now, because the ordering and quoting is exactly what AI eats. They'd be hit before me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the safer ones for a while. No robot is swinging a crane over a garden wall on Mill Lane any time soon. But the yard office would shrink, and that means fewer people, more mistakes on my delivery notes, and me sorting them out on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever system they bring in for delivery notes and routes, properly, so I'm the one who helps the others. I'd get the supervisor ticket done in the first year. I'd also nudge Priya to look at training as a full teacher, because one of us needs a step up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for my mates in the office, a bit protective of my own spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra, who's done the quotes and orders for thirty years and knows every builder by their first name. She's the reason half our trade customers stay. A computer would do her job faster and lose the customers slowly without anyone noticing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd nudge Priya. What would that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her training would mean a year on less money, maybe two. We'd need to be careful, no holidays, my car running on prayers. But I'd rather do that than both of us stay stuck on low pay.

say: People who do the **lifting** deserve a fair share of what firms save.
I'd tell the yard office staff to **join the union** now.
think: No robot will swing a **crane** over a garden wall any time soon.
A shrinking office means more **mistakes** on my delivery notes.
do: Learn the new **delivery system** well enough to help the others.
Finish the **supervisor ticket** in the first year.
Encourage my partner to train as a **full teacher**.
feel: **Uneasy** for office colleagues and **protective** of his own place.
S1.quote: A computer would do Sandra's job faster and lose the customers slowly without anyone noticing.
fieldNote: He sees desk jobs at the yard going **first** and his crane work later.
His solidarity is practical: he tells colleagues to **unionise early**.
Ready to accept a year of **lower income** so his partner can step up.

steps.text: Learn the new delivery note system and teach the other drivers
Finish the crane supervisor ticket this year
Back Priya through teacher training on one income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a proper safety net, universal basic income or something like it, and I'd say it everywhere. I'd be at the union branch every month. Two years is no time at all for ordinary people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have five years till a robot crane truck does my work, and less till the yard office is gone completely. Five years sounds like a lot, but with three weeks of savings it's nothing. I don't know what a crane driver becomes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending except rent and food and push every spare pound into savings. I'd start asking around about jobs that need hands and judgement together, maybe maintenance on whatever robot machines they bring in. I'd also look seriously at whether Priya and I move back near my mum's to cut rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like being told a storm's coming and our roof is already leaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean for your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork and route planning would go to software right away, so my day would become just lifting and driving. For three years I'd be the hands for a computer's brain. Then the hands go too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you moved near your mum, what would you lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya's school, which she loves, and my mates from the yard. My mum's town has even fewer driving jobs than here. It'd be a move to survive, not to get ahead.

say: This is the moment for a **safety net**, like universal basic income.
Two years is **no time** for ordinary families to prepare.
think: Robot crane trucks would arrive in **five years**, the office sooner.
With **three weeks** of savings, five years feels like nothing.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** and save the rest.
Ask about **robot maintenance** jobs that need hands and judgement.
Consider moving near **my mum** to cut rent.
feel: **Alarmed**, like a storm coming with the roof already **leaking**.
S2.quote: For three years I'd be the hands for a computer's brain.
fieldNote: He describes the **three-year gap** vividly: thinking work goes, lifting stays briefly.
A move near family would be **survival**, not progress, and would cost his partner her school.
Public call for **basic income** matches his private fear.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food and save every spare pound
Ask around about robot maintenance work needing hands-on judgement
Look at renting near his mum's town to cut costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this right, if governments actually bother. I'd want free retraining and a law that firms share savings from robots with workers. I'd bang on about it at the pub and the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, eight years before the crane truck is automated gives me a fair shot. I'd be thirty-five, which is young enough to learn a new trade. It's the first few years of not knowing which trade that worry me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the supervisor ticket in year one, then start an evening course in electrical installation in year two, because something has to wire all these machines up. I'd keep driving full time to pay the rent. I'd try out AI tools for studying, since lots of the lads say it helps with the theory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but with a plan forming, which helps more than I'd expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle's a sparky and he's never short of work. And it's hands-on, which I'm good at, and it's in people's houses, which robots will find harder. I'm not sure it's safe forever, but it buys years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you afford an evening course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college has a payment plan, about forty a month. I'd skip the football season ticket. Priya would grumble about me never being home, then she'd test me on the theory.

say: Five years is **enough time** if governments actually bother.
Firms should **share savings** from robots with workers by law.
think: Eight years before automation gives me a **fair shot** at a new trade.
Not knowing **which trade** worries me more than the change itself.
do: Finish the **supervisor ticket** in year one.
Start an evening **electrical installation** course in year two.
Use **AI tools** to help with the course theory.
feel: **Anxious**, but a forming **plan** helps more than expected.
S3.quote: My uncle's a sparky and he's never short of work.
fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a **step-by-step plan**.
He chooses **electrical work** for being hands-on and in homes, where robots may struggle.
Pays for it by giving up the **football season ticket**.

steps.text: Finish the crane supervisor ticket in year one
Start an evening electrical installation course on a payment plan
Drop the football season ticket to pay course fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say there's no excuse for anyone to be left behind, and I'd hold politicians to it. I'd tell the young drivers at the yard to plan their second trade now. I'd sound like my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I could drive until about thirty-eight, then switch. That's a decent stretch. The worry is that everyone has the same idea and the trades fill up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd mostly carry on, get the supervisor ticket and build savings properly, aiming for two months. I'd go to an open evening at the college about electrical courses but probably start in a few years. I'd vote for whoever has a real plan for workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a slow, background way. Like knowing you'll need a new boiler eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everyone might have the same idea. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get in early, I suppose, around year three or four, before the rush. And pick something with a licence, so you can't just turn up and do it. The lads who wait will be fighting for scraps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya and I would probably think about kids around then, so it matters. I wouldn't want to retrain with a baby in the house. That's partly why I'd start the course earlier than I need to.

say: Ten years means **no excuse** for leaving anyone behind.
I'd tell young drivers to plan a **second trade** now.
think: I could drive until about **thirty-eight**, then switch.
Everyone might have the same idea and **trades fill up**.
do: Finish the supervisor ticket and save **two months** in year one.
Attend a college **open evening** on electrical courses.
Vote for whoever has a **real plan** for workers.
feel: **Anxious** in a slow background way, like a boiler you'll need eventually.
S4.quote: I wouldn't want to retrain with a baby in the house.
fieldNote: He links career timing to **having children**, which pulls retraining earlier.
Worries less about robots than about **crowded trades** once everyone moves.
Ten years softens the tone but he still expects to **lose the crane job**.

steps.text: Save two months of bills by the end of year one
Go to the college open evening on electrical courses
Vote for candidates with a real plan for workers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because we'd have nothing saved and no time to train. What would help is a living wage while you retrain, so I could do the electrical course full time instead of over four years of evenings. And proper housing costs, because rent is what keeps us on the edge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the builders think. They trust me because I've never dropped a load in six years. I don't know if they'll trust a robot crane over their new conservatory, and that trust might buy drivers like me a bit more time.

headlineQuote: No robot is swinging a crane over a garden wall on Mill Lane any time soon.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old** crane flatbed driver for a builders' merchant, senior and trusted on site.
He rents with his partner, a teaching assistant, and has about **three weeks** of savings.
Progressive and practical, he urges office staff to **unionise** and backs a safety net.
He moves from uneasy to alarmed under fast AGI, steadying as he plans an **electrical trade**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no savings and no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **living wage** while retraining, so he could study full time.
Lower **housing costs**, since rent keeps the household on the edge.
